- When catalog sources are projected, existing catalog, projection and instruction-size checks shall pass without raising caps or weakening gates.

When the projected always-on baseline mixes prose and constraints with no fixed structure, I want the constraint content projected as an explicit three-tier block, so I can make the rules easier to retrieve and follow.

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-30 by applying oh-my-openagent's forbidden-token gate idea to our own projected output
(`reference-repos/_analysis/oh-my-openagent.md`).

`.github/copilot-instructions.md:9` and `AGENTS.md:9` both carry:

> Force-push, history rewrite, destructive resets, `rm -rf`, and `.env*` reads/writes - hard-denied
> in `.claude/settings.json` for Claude Code; this rule covers other agents, so treat a blocked
> command as the answer.

`CLAUDE.md` does **not** carry it, so per-target variation already exists and is deliberate: the
Claude file omits the sentence because for Claude the deny-list is the actual mechanism rather than
something to describe.

The inverse is the defect. Copilot and any `AGENTS.md` reader are told about a file they will never
read and a mechanism that does not apply to them, then told the rule covers them anyway. The
author clearly considered it - the "this rule covers other agents" clause is there on purpose - so
this is imprecise wording rather than an oversight, and it is mild.

**Stated at its real size:** this is not a secrets leak and nothing sensitive is disclosed;
`.claude/settings.json` is a committed file. The cost is a sentence of always-on baseline spent
telling an agent about another agent's enforcement, in a baseline already measured at cap
(`always-on-baseline-at-cap`). The fix is to state the rule in terms of the reader - a blocked
command is the answer - and let the Claude target alone carry the mechanism.

Worth generalising while in there: whether any other fragment names one target's mechanism inside
another target's output. A cheap catalog-lint rule could check that a fragment body rendered into
target X does not reference target Y's config path, which is the transferable half of the
forbidden-token idea.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the projected instruction files when the confirmation-rules fragment is rendered then no target's output names another target's config path or enforcement mechanism, and the rule reads as a constraint on the agent reading it

payload.description:
## Context

Retro finding from the 2026-07-30 session, approved by the owner and filed rather than self-applied
per the repo's retro rule. **Three distinct failures in one session share one root cause: reviewing an
external project without discipline.** All three reached committed files before being corrected.

1. **A README is a claim; the binary is the evidence.** I wrote into
   `docs/research/2026-07-26-sota-review.md` §2.11 that gastown ships a Bors-style merge queue that
   bisects to isolate a failing MR, and recommended building the same - from a fetched README summary.
   It is dead code: `AssembleBatch`/`ProcessBatch` have no call sites outside tests, the config field
   that enables them is never read, and the Go merge engine cannot be entered because its foreground
   mode hard-errors as deprecated while the real component is an agent working the queue sequentially.
   The corrected conclusion **inverted** the original.
2. **Read the licence before writing the adopt finding, not after.** In the same commit I wrote the
   warning that "deriving an implementation from a quoted snippet requires reading that project's
   LICENSE first" and then recommended porting ~400 lines from two repos whose licences had not been
   read. Both were restricted, and in **both cases the LICENSE file alone would have cleared them** -
   one hid a non-commercial Sustainable Use License with a per-subdirectory gap, the other put
   competition restrictions in `NOTICE.md`. That is three restricted repos in this reference set now.
3. **Correlation is not causation, and synthesis is where they get confused.** I wrote that every
   project adopting declarative phases traded away determinism, implying cause. Both failures were
   independent design errors in projects that also happened to be configurable. The decision to reject
   still held, on a different and better argument.

## The rules to record

- Before recommending adoption of a third-party feature, find its call sites; a symbol with no
  non-test caller does not ship, and neither does one behind a config flag nobody reads. Cite
  `file:line`, never a README line.
- Read every licence-bearing file including `NOTICE`, and check per-directory licences before assuming
  a monorepo is uniform - **before** writing adopt findings.
- A licence restricts copying expression, not learning a fact: measurements and concepts survive a
  restriction, implementations do not. That boundary is what keeps a competitive review usable.
- When a pattern appears across independent sources, state whether the mechanism is established or
  only the correlation.

## The open decision this bead must make, not assume

**Where these live is deliberately unsettled.** The obvious answer is a new on-demand skill
(`external-review` or similar), which costs nothing always-on - and the always-on baseline is at cap,
so that matters. But adding a 28th catalog skill is the wrong reflex right now: 27 existing skills have
never been invoked, and whether skills route at all is `basicly-m4zv.2`'s open question. Weigh at least
these before authoring anything:

- a new on-demand skill - zero always-on cost, but grows a catalog whose routing is unmeasured;
- a section in an existing skill - `catalog-authoring` is the closest fit and is already always-on for
  Copilot by a recorded decision;
- the **path-scoped rules tier**, which is built and almost unused, if a path predicate can express
  "editing a research or design document";
- prose in `docs/research/references.md` §2 only, accepting that a rule not in the catalog does not
  reach an agent that has not read that file.

Do not add always-on baseline text for this without measuring the delta - the tier exists precisely so
this class of conditional guidance costs nothing when it does not apply.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the four external-review rules when their home has been chosen and justified against the always-on baseline cost then they are authored in that home, projected, and an agent reviewing a third-party repository is told to verify call sites and read licences before writing an adopt finding
payload.title: Record the external-review rules that three committed errors would have prevented

Known cost accepted: codex inlines scoped fragments so AGENTS.md grows (8484 of 12000 today); measure and record the delta per this bead's AC. A new skill was rejected because 27 skills have never routed and routing is unmeasured until basicly-m4zv.2.

payload.description:
## Context

Retro finding from the 2026-07-30 session, approved by the owner and filed rather than self-applied.
An environment trap, so it earns exactly one bullet: the trap plus its avoidance.

**The incident.** Removing seventeen deferred blocking edges from the release epic, I wrote:

```sh
DEFER="basicly-jr0l.35 basicly-jr0l.40 ..."
for d in $DEFER; do uv run br dep remove basicly-m3od "$d"; done
```

In bash that iterates seventeen times. **This repo's shell is zsh, which does not word-split an
unquoted parameter expansion**, so the loop ran once with all seventeen ids as a single argument. The
command failed, and the failure was quiet in the way that matters: the loop printed one line, the
summary said `removed 0`, and only a separate re-count of the edges revealed nothing had happened. Had
I trusted the exit status or the absence of an error, the release scope would silently still be blocked
by seventeen beads.

**The avoidance**: write the list inline in the `for` header, or use an array (`arr=(a b c)` then
`for d in "${arr[@]}"`), or pipe through `xargs -n1`. Never iterate an unquoted scalar and assume
splitting.

**Why this is worth a catalog bullet rather than a note.** `non-interactive-shell.fragment.yaml`
already owns exactly this class - it exists because some shells alias `cp`/`mv`/`rm` to interactive
mode - and the fragment's own framing is "prefer cross-platform implementations over shell-specific
behavior when a choice exists". Word-splitting is the same shape: a construct that is correct in one
shell and silently wrong in another, on a repo that targets Windows, Linux and macOS and whose own
hooks run under whatever shell the host provides.

It also compounds with an existing recorded trap - `uv run` inside a shell for-loop returning empty
output, which already made a per-item audit report "all clean" falsely
(`batch-queries-over-cli-loops`). Both failures are the same lesson from different directions: a
shell loop over a list is where a silent no-op hides, so prefer one batch invocation and verify the
count changed.

**Cost check before authoring.** This fragment is always-on and the baseline is at cap, so keep it to
one bullet and measure the delta rather than adding a paragraph.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the non-interactive-shell guidance when it is read after this change then it warns that an unquoted parameter expansion does not word-split in every shell, names the array or inline-list avoidance, and the always-on baseline delta is measured and recorded
payload.title: Warn that an unquoted list does not word-split in every shell

payload.description:
## Context

Owner, 2026-08-09: "the code always has authority, not comments; comments that describe the
code must not exist, outside of best practices. If you need to read the comments to understand
the code, then the code is not of adequate quality, too complex, and potentially hard to
maintain." Proposed as an always-on rule.

**It conflicts with this repository's current practice**, which is the reason it needs research
rather than adoption. src/ and .basicly/core/ are deliberately and heavily commented, and most
comments explain *why* a thing is the way it is rather than what it does. factory-loop section
9.2 already carries the weaker form - "a docstring restating the signature passes and is
worthless" - and the proposed rule is stronger than that.

So the research question is not "are explanatory comments bad" in the abstract. It is: **which
comments does the evidence actually condemn, and does this repo's population fall inside or
outside that set.**

## What must be established

- What PEP 8, PEP 257 and the CPython developer guide actually prescribe, quoted, not
  paraphrased. Distinguish what they mandate from what they suggest.
- Whether the "self-documenting code needs no comments" position has empirical support or is
  a repeated assertion. Look for measurement, not for essays citing essays.
- The distinction the literature draws between what-comments, why-comments, contract comments
  and provenance comments, since the owner's rule targets the first and this repo's population
  is mostly the second and fourth.
- What the ruff, pyright and pydocstyle rule sets already enforce here, so a new rule does not
  restate a gate we already run.
- Ask why until the answer stops changing, and record the branch not taken. The repo already
  holds a sourced caution on iterated-why (Card, BMJ Quality and Safety 2017) so the method
  has to answer its own literature.

## Deliverable

A verdict with sources, and one of: the exact fragment text to add, an amendment to the
existing section 9.2 line, or a recorded decision not to add a rule with the reason. Per D25
an agent never lands catalog guidance without a human.

## Method

Dispatch the `researcher` agent authored in this session. It is projected to both agent
families but does not load until the host process restarts.
payload.title: Verify the comments-versus-code rule against authoritative sources before making it always-on

payload.text:
RESEARCHED AND DECIDED 2026-08-09. Verdict: reject the strong form, adopt the divergence rule.
Landed as D34 in docs/requirements/factory-loop.md section 2, with section 9.2 item 3 amended and
item 10 added. Implementation is basicly-a3ab.9.

Four independent grounds, any one sufficient:

1. It targets an empty set here. 120-block hand sample over src/basicly and .basicly/core:
   41% contract, 40% why, 16% navigation, 3% directive, 0% NARRATION. Two whole-population probes,
   each validated against synthetic narration first: narration-opener regex 0 of 1389 while catching
   5 of 5 synthetics; code-echo >= 0.50 gives 9 of 1139, every one a cross-reference.
2. The strong form contradicts PEP 8, which MANDATES a describe-what comment for non-public methods.
   Google's "never describe the code" - which .ruff.toml already pins via convention = "google" -
   is stated immediately after a REQUIREMENT to comment complicated operations.
3. It arms a live gaming path. Stripping standalone comments returns 36.3% of config.py's section
   9.3 ratchet tokens, 17.0% of merge.py's (frozen at exactly its current count) and 11.6% of
   loop.py's. python-guidelines/skill.yaml:72 already names comment deletion as the way to game that
   gate.
4. No budget. AGENTS.md is 13135 chars against codex.yaml's 12000 cap, and the parent epic exists to
   RELIEVE the always-on layer. Filed as basicly-a3ab.10.

Not agent-actionable either: "outside of best practices" is an undefined exemption and "if you need
to read the comments" is a counterfactual about a reader the agent cannot query. Neither is
falsifiable. Divergence is - did this diff change a line whose comment still describes the old
behaviour.

The literature does not settle it. "Comments are always failures" traces to Clean Code ch.4, a trade
book with no cited study. Measured work is mixed: Nielebock et al. 2018 (n=277) "the real effect of
comments on software development remains uncertain"; a 2026 eye-tracking study (n=20) spans a 30%
decrease to a 34% increase.

CORRECTS THIS BEAD'S OWN PREMISE: the body claims this repo's comments are mostly why and provenance
comments. Measured, the largest class is CONTRACT at 41%, why at 40%, and provenance is not a class
at all but a modifier present on 31.7% of blocks across classes. The conclusion survives; the stated
proportions do not, and 0% narration is a stronger claim than the one asserted.

BRANCH NOT TAKEN (Card 2017): that the owner is right and density is a symptom - that config.py
being 36% comments argues for decomposition, not annotation. Partial support exists (over-cap median
9.9 per 100 code lines vs 7.6 under-cap) but it is confounded by age and size. Filed as OQ-17.

Three measurements independently re-derived by the session before landing.

Requirements landed 2026-08-09 as D34/D35 in docs/requirements/factory-loop.md section 2, with

## Scope

- Add `paths: ["**/*.py"]` to the same skill source per D35.
- If schemas/skill.schema.json does not yet carry `paths`, add it, fenced as claude-only if the
  projection needs that - copilot honours it, codex has no glob scoping at all.

## Constraint

D25: this is catalog guidance, so the diff goes to a human. Do not land it under a grant.

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly skills-check --all-default-roots` is green, the projected
.claude/skills/python-guidelines/SKILL.md carries the paths front matter, and touching any .py file
in a fresh session loads the skill without it being named.

payload.text:
SPLIT 2026-08-09. D34 is done; D35 is blocked on a design decision this bead assumed away.

D34 LANDED in a684dd4: the "Comments - the divergence rule" section is in
.basicly/core/skills/python-guidelines/skill.yaml and projected to both roots. Full suite 3580
passed, all six projection gates green.

D35 IS NOT DONE, and the bead's assumption that it is a front matter line is wrong.

.basicly/core/schemas/skill.schema.json carries exactly ten properties with
`additionalProperties: false`, and the six spec-portable ones are deliberately the Agent Skills
portable subset - name, description, license, compatibility, metadata, allowed-tools - which the
2026-08-09 research confirmed against the vendor documentation. `paths:` is NOT in that subset. It
is claude-only, copilot honours it, and codex has no glob scoping at all.

src/basicly/schema.py has a `scope_paths` field, but it belongs to FRAGMENTS, not skills.
skills.py `_optional_frontmatter` emits only the four optional spec fields.

So adding `paths:` needs a vendor-fence mechanism for skill front matter that does not exist today,
and inventing one inline would put an unportable key into the artifact whose portability is the
reason the schema is shaped this way.

## The decision this now needs

Either add a `claude:` (or per-target) fence to the skill schema and teach the renderer to emit
fenced keys only into the roots that understand them, or decide that skill front matter stays
strictly portable and path scoping is expressed some other way.

Both are catalog-architecture calls, so they belong to a human under D25 rather than being picked
here. Whichever wins, D35's stated benefit is unchanged: zero always-on characters, and no
dependency on basicly-a3ab.1's eviction.

payload.description:
Found shipping basicly-ajq. loop._build_children fan-in merges every child worktree via merge.merge_queue once all children are closed — but a child driven through its own loop (the flow the harness-loop skill documents: advance lands the worktree, ship tears it down and closes) leaves no worktree behind, so the parent's advance fails with "no worktree session named '<child>'" and the feature can never advance past build. Workaround used: record the parent verify gate directly (basicly verify --mode full --issue <id>), then approve ship and loop run.

Two coherent fixes; pick one and align the harness-loop skill with it:
(a) parent skips children whose branches are already merged (self-landing stays the documented child flow), or
(b) children stop self-landing (their loop ends at 'work committed'; the parent owns the merge queue) and the skill/docs change accordingly.

Chosen: (a) — in loop._build_children, filter merge-queue items to children with a live worktree session (worktree.list_sessions()); self-landed torn-down children count as already landed and are mentioned in the detail message.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a feature issue with two child tasks (br create --parent).
2. Drive each child through its own full loop: advance provisions its worktree, build/verify pass, advance lands the worktree, ship tears it down and closes the child.
3. With all children closed and no child worktree sessions remaining, run `basicly loop advance <parent>` to trigger the build fan-in.
4. Observed: SystemExit "no worktree session named '<child>'" from merge.merge_queue; the feature can never advance past build. Expected: fan-in treats the self-landed children as already merged and advances build -> verify.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A feature whose children each landed and closed through their own loop advances build -> verify without manual gate recording
- merge_queue (or its caller) treats an already-merged, torn-down child as satisfied rather than an error
- A regression test covers the children-self-landed path
- The harness-loop skill's phase table matches the implemented flow

payload.description:
## Context

Filed 2026-07-31 after basicly-kjc5.58 landed. **Re-scoped the same day by the owner, who was right and
the first framing was wrong**: this is NOT claude-only. GitHub Copilot custom agents carry a per-agent
`model` field too, so at least claude AND copilot must be supported. Re-verified against live
authoritative docs rather than recall.

basicly-kjc5.59 is the resolution seam but its scope is `runner.py`/`run_record.py`/`config.py` - the
HEADLESS runner dispatch path, where a model is set by `_apply_model` via a `--model` flag or a
`{model}` placeholder. A natively spawned subagent never goes through that path: the host reads a
per-agent file and takes the model from frontmatter. basicly-kjc5.58 removed that line for every
family, so a declared tier is currently decorative for every natively spawned agent.

Concrete regression from kjc5.58, deliberate and known: the shipped `test-runner` declared
`model: haiku`, now declares `tier: low`, and `.claude/agents/test-runner.md` carries no model line, so
an agent whose own prose says "cheap and fast on purpose" inherits the session model on every spawn.
Verified: `rg '^model' .claude/agents/` matches nothing.

kjc5.58 was still right - the defect was a NON-PORTABLE value in a family-agnostic source. The fix is
to emit the resolved per-surface spelling, which is what basicly-kjc5.61's map must provide.

## Verified facts (live docs, 2026-07-31)

- **Claude Code** reads `.claude/agents/<slug>.md`; `model` takes a hyphenated id (`claude-haiku-4-5`)
  or a short alias (`haiku`), or `inherit`.
- **GitHub Copilot** custom agents live at `.github/agents/<name>.agent.md` (org/enterprise: root
  `agents/`). Frontmatter: `description` (required), `name`, `target` (`vscode`|`github-copilot`),
  `tools`, `model`, `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`, `mcp-servers`, `metadata`; body
  capped at 30000 chars, which `agents.MAX_BODY_CHARS` already matches.
- **Copilot's `model` value is a DISPLAY NAME**, not an id - `Claude Opus 4.5`, `Claude Sonnet 4` -
  and it accepts **a single string OR a prioritized array** tried in order
  (`model: ['Claude Opus 4.5', 'GPT-5.2']`). Our schema cannot express an ordered fallback list today.
- **VS Code reads BOTH** `.github/agents` and `.claude/agents` ("VS Code also detects `.md` files in the
  `.claude/agents` folder, following the Claude sub-agents format"). So basicly-ajq's rationale holds
  for VS Code but NOT for the Copilot cloud agent or Copilot CLI, which do not read `.claude/agents`.
- Copilot `tools` names differ from Claude's and are inconsistent across sources
  (`["read","search","edit"]` in the VS Code doc vs `codebase`/`terminal`/`edit`/`github` elsewhere), so
  a copilot projection needs a pinned tool-name mapping, not a copy.

## Prerequisite

The copilot half has no target file today: basicly still projects to `.claude/agents` only. Reopening
that is filed separately and must land first for the copilot half. The claude half is unblocked once
kjc5.61 lands.

## Open design decision for the owner

Per surface, either resolve the tier to that surface's own spelling and emit it, or emit nothing and
record that the tier was not honoured (the stance kjc5.59 already takes where a family has no slot).
Recommendation: resolve and emit wherever the surface has a model slot, because that is the only case
in which the tier vocabulary changes real behaviour instead of documenting an intention.

Scope: `src/basicly/agents.py`, `.claude/agents/`, `tests/test_agents.py`.
payload.title: Resolve a declared tier into each projected agent surface that has a model slot

payload.text: DYNAMIC INJECTION IS POSSIBLE ON CLAUDE CODE - PROVEN BY EXPERIMENT 2026-07-31. The owner asked whether the model could be left out of the projected file and injected before the host reads it, rather than baked in at build time. Answer: YES for claude code, via a PreToolUse hook on the Agent tool. Three probes, each isolated with 'claude --settings <file>' so no live config was modified: (1) returning updatedInput {model: haiku} alone FAILED - the call lost its required fields; (2) returning updatedInput {description: ...} alone also FAILED with 'required parameter prompt is missing'. So on the Agent tool updatedInput REPLACES tool_input rather than merging, which CONTRADICTS the documented behaviour 'Object with fields to merge into tool_input ... Fields not present in updatedInput are left unchanged'. Worth knowing: that doc statement is false for this tool. (3) The working pattern - copy the whole tool_input dict, add model, return the lot - SUCCEEDED. Proof it took effect: the probe agent's frontmatter declared model: opus, the hook injected haiku, and the subagent's own transcript under projects/<proj>/<session><redacted:posix-absolute-path>*.jsonl carries 22 messages all with model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, with ZERO occurrences of opus in any transcript of the run. The frontmatter was overridden. This is consistent with the documented resolution order, where the per-invocation model parameter (2) outranks the definition's frontmatter (3). Observed Agent tool_input keys: description, prompt, subagent_type, run_in_background - note model is ABSENT unless the caller sets it, which is why it must be added rather than rewritten. Robustness note: because the hook copies the input dict wholesale it forwards unknown and future fields verbatim, so a new required field upstream does not break it. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS BEAD: there are now two viable mechanisms, not one. Static emission at agents-build time (this bead as originally scoped) OR a hook that resolves tier to model at spawn time from the committed map, leaving the projected file model-free. The hook variant is strictly more portable - a foreign harness needs only the map plus a ~15 line hook and no basicly code at all, which is the owner's stated plug-and-play goal - but it adds a process to the spawn path and is claude-code-specific as verified. The copilot equivalent is NOT yet verified: copilot custom agents and copilot CLI both document a hooks field (Preview) and that needs its own probe before any claim. Do not assume symmetry.

COPILOT CLI HOOK INJECTION DOES NOT WORK TODAY - tested 2026-07-31 at the owner's request. Copilot DOES document the capability: the hooks reference gives preToolUse an output schema of permissionDecision (allow|deny|ask), permissionDecisionReason, and modifiedArgs described as 'tool arguments to use instead of the originals' - i.e. argument substitution is specified. Documented CLI config locations: repo-level .github/hooks/NAME.json, user-level ~/.copilot/hooks/ (or COPILOT_HOME), plus policy.d and inline settings. BUT on the installed CLI the hook never fires. Three probes from a scratch repo containing .github/hooks/tierprobe.json with a preToolUse command hook that logged every payload and returned allow: (1) delegating to a custom agent - hook did not fire; (2) a plain shell tool with --allow-all-tools - did not fire; (3) the same shell tool WITHOUT --allow-all-tools, to rule out the permission pipeline being bypassed - did not fire. Zero payloads captured in any run, so this is not about which tool is intercepted; the repo-level hook config is simply not being loaded or run. Note 'hook' does not appear anywhere in copilot --help, and experimental was already true in settings. LIKELY EXPLANATION, not yet confirmed: the modifiedArgs capability is documented under the copilot-SDK hooks path (<redacted:posix-absolute-path>), so it may be an SDK-only feature rather than a CLI one. Do not assume the CLI will grow it. VERSION DRIFT WORTH KNOWING: the binary reported 1.0.75 earlier in the same session and 1.0.77 by the end - it self-updates, so a pinned version in prose rots by itself and per-run adapter_version capture (which the runner already does) is the right design. WHAT DOES WORK ON COPILOT: static frontmatter. Verified twice - the /agent listing validated a declared model value, and a custom agent declaring NO model printed 'Tierprobe(claude-opus-5)' in the CLI transcript, i.e. it inherited the session model. Also note copilot prints the resolved model in its delegation line, which is a free observation channel for verifying any future mechanism. CONSEQUENCE: for a first version the mechanism is necessarily HYBRID - claude gets dynamic hook injection (proven working), copilot gets static frontmatter emission (proven working) plus session-level control via copilot --model for harness-launched sessions. That is not the uniform design the owner would prefer but it is what the two hosts actually support today.

CORRECTION - COPILOT HOOK INJECTION DOES WORK. The earlier comment on this bead concluded copilot CLI hooks never fire. That was WRONG, and the cause was the config LOCATION, not the capability. Repo-level .github/hooks/hooks.json is NOT loaded by copilot CLI 1.0.77 (retested with the canonical filename, with inline bash instead of a script path, and inside a real git repo - sessionStart did not fire either, so it was not about tool matching). User-level ~/.copilot/hooks/hooks.json IS loaded and fires. Also retracted: I claimed the CLI binary contains no hook identifiers based on a strings scan. That evidence was worthless - a control check showed strings I had directly observed the CLI emitting (allow-all-tools, premiumRequests, modelMetrics) also return zero matches, because the JS payload is a compressed bundle. The conclusion rests on behaviour only. PROVEN END TO END on copilot: the agent-spawn tool is named 'task' with args agent_type, description, mode, name, prompt - and NO model key, so model must be ADDED not rewritten, same as claude. A preToolUse hook matching toolName 'task' that returns modifiedArgs containing all original args PLUS model ran a custom agent declaring NO model on the injected model: the CLI delegation line printed Tierprobe(claude-haiku-4.5) where the session model was claude-opus-5. Copilot prints the resolved model in that line, which is a free verification channel. PER-HOST DIFFERENCES to encode: hook event PreToolUse vs preToolUse; tool name Agent vs task; rewrite field updatedInput vs modifiedArgs; payload tool_input as an OBJECT vs toolArgs as a JSON STRING that must be parsed first; model spelling claude-haiku-4-5 or the alias haiku vs the dotted claude-haiku-4.5; observation channel the subagent transcript vs the printed delegation line. Both REPLACE rather than merge, so both hooks must echo the full argument set back. IMPORTANT DESIGN CONSTRAINT for basicly-wbsz: because copilot only honours the hook at USER level, it applies to every repo on the machine. So the hook cannot assume a map is present - it must resolve against the current working directory and NO-OP silently, leaving the call untouched, whenever the cwd has no committed map. It also cannot be delivered by repo projection the way our other artifacts are; it needs a per-machine install step.

FINDING 2026-09-16, from dogfooding the tier kit in this repository.

The hook is now installed here. `python3 .basicly/core/kit/tier/install_hook.py` exits 0 and writes the `PreToolUse`/`Agent` entry into `.claude/settings.json`, project scope. The earlier note saying the claude installer declines with a nonzero exit was false and is withdrawn.

**Installing it changes nothing, and the cause is upstream of the hook.** Fed a real spawn payload the hook returns no rewrite for `reviewer`, `implementer` and `validator` alike, and the resolver says why:

    $ python3 .basicly/core/kit/tier/tier_resolver.py --host claude --name reviewer
    {"alias": null, "model": null, "reason": "no tier is declared for this spawn and no default tier is configured", ...}

**The catalog source declares the tier and the projector drops it.** `.basicly/core/agents/reviewer/agent.yaml` line 8 reads `tier: high`. **0 of 11 projected files under `.claude/agents/` carry a `tier:` field.** `agents.py:224` parses `tier` into the agent model and `agents.py:434` validates it against `MODEL_TIERS`, and nothing emits it into the rendered frontmatter. The resolver reads the projected file, so it reads a file the tier never reached.

So the sentence "the tier is declared on every agent source and validated by lint, and it reaches no spawn" is right about the ends and wrong about the middle: the break is at projection, not at spawn. Installing a hook, wiring a host or probing whether the hook fires cannot move this until a projected agent file carries its tier.

COST OF LEAVING THE HOOK INSTALLED: one `uv run` subprocess per Agent spawn, for no effect until the projection carries the tier. It is correct-and-inert rather than wrong, and it becomes live the moment the field is emitted. Remove the `Agent` matcher from `.claude/settings.json` to revert.

NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the host actually calls the hook on a spawn. Every probe here fed the script a payload directly. That question stays open and needs one real spawn against an agent whose projected file carries a tier, which does not exist yet.

SHIPPED 2026-09-16, commit 8a2b89ff. The chain from a declared tier to a spawn now closes, and one real spawn proves it.

PROOF, not assertion. `claude -p` was told to spawn the `validator` subagent, which declares `tier: medium`, from a session whose lead runs Opus. The result object's `modelUsage` carries `claude-opus-5[1m]` for the lead and **`claude-sonnet-5`** for the subagent. The hook fired and rewrote the spawn. 0.43 usd list.

FOUR CHANGES.

1. **The projector emits `tier:`** (`agents.render_agent_md`). Every one of the 11 agents now carries its tier into both `.claude/agents/<slug>.md` and `.github/agents/<slug>.agent.md`. `tier` joins `RESERVED_FRONTMATTER_KEYS`, so a `claude:` passthrough cannot shadow it and the source stays the one declaration.

2. **`basicly install` wires the host** - a `tier-hook` step after `hooks-build` runs the kit's own `install_hook.py` against the repository. It reports and continues rather than failing the install, because a repository without the kit is a normal repository.

3. **`basicly-tier init` wires the host too.** `Kit` gained `configure_file`; the installer runs it from the **vendored** copy after the files land, so the hook command names `.basicly/kit/tier/claude_tier_hook.py` rather than a catalog path the consumer does not have.

4. **The vendored map is found.** `find_map` walked only for `<base><redacted:posix-absolute-path>`, which a standalone consumer never has, so the hook silently declined. It now falls back to the map beside the kit **when the kit sits inside the project being resolved**.

THE SAFETY PROPERTY THAT SHAPED (4), AND THE BUG MY FIRST ATTEMPT INTRODUCED. `test_a_directory_with_no_map_is_left_alone_though_the_kit_has_one_beside_it` exists because a `--user` scope hook must not rewrite spawns in a project that never opted in. My first fix flipped `beside_the_kit` and broke it. The second attempt scoped the fallback to `here.is_relative_to(base)` inside the ancestor walk, and the negative regression test I wrote caught that this still leaks: a kit in `~/dev/repoA` answered for `~/dev/repoB`, because both are under `~/dev`. The landed rule compares against `start` alone, so the kit answers only for the project it sits inside. Both cases are now pinned - `test_a_vendored_kit_reads_the_map_it_installed_beside_itself` and `test_a_vendored_kit_leaves_a_project_it_was_not_installed_into_alone`.

WHY A FRONTMATTER KEY AND NOT A SIDECAR, MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. Neither vendor documents what happens to an unknown frontmatter key, so both were probed on 2026-09-16. Claude: an agent carrying `tier: high` loaded beside a clean one, both present in `system/init` among 7 agents, no warning. Copilot CLI 1.0.83: `copilot -p --agent <name>` exited 0 for an agent with a bare `tier:` key and for one carrying it inside the documented `metadata:` field. One shape was chosen over per-host shapes because the resolver's frontmatter reader is a five-line regex in a stdlib-only kit, and Copilot's `metadata` is the documented upgrade path if the bare key ever breaks.

D-09 IS NOT TOUCHED. It refuses a provider model id in an agent file and says a projected `model:` line would disable injection. A tier is neither an id nor a pin, and the new test asserts `"claude-" not in rendered` beside `"tier: maximum" in rendered`.

GATES. `uv run pytest -q` 5776 passed 1 xfailed. `uv run basicly verify --mode full` All checks passed. `kit-boundary` passes - an earlier draft named `.basicly/kit/tier` as a literal and the gate correctly refused it as an engine read; the kit now derives its own location from `__file__`. One `# noqa: S603` is frozen in `basicly.d/basicly-a3yi.toml`, because architecture section 5 keeps the engine free of kit imports, so the installer is run rather than loaded.

STILL OPEN. `uninstall` does not remove the hook, so a removed kit leaves a settings entry pointing at a missing file. Copilot has no spawn hook wired; that host carries per-subagent selection in config and basicly-u2hl.41 owns it. Whether a Copilot spawn honours the projected tier is unproven

PROVEN FOR IN-SESSION BACKGROUND SPAWNS 2026-09-16, and the uninstall defect is closed. Commit 2b140ec0.

THE SPAWN PATH THE EARLIER PROOF DID NOT COVER. The first proof used `claude -p`, which left open whether the hook reaches a subagent an interactive session spawns. It does, and the evidence is two-step rather than inferred.

1. **The host calls the hook for an in-session background spawn.** A second `PreToolUse`/`Agent` hook that only appended its payload to a file was installed beside the tier hook, a background `tester` subagent was spawned from a live session, and the log recorded `{"tool": "Agent", "subagent_type": "tester", "model_in_input": null}`. The trace hook was removed afterwards and `.claude/settings.json` restored byte-identical, confirmed by an empty `git status` on that path.

2. **The rewrite is applied, not merely offered.** The background subagent's own transcript carries the model on every assistant message: **`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`, on all 7 of them**, while the lead session runs Opus. `tester` declares `tier: low`, which resolves to `haiku`. Nothing but the hook could have moved that spawn off the lead's model.

The session transcript is the wrong instrument for this and was tried first. It records the `Agent` tool_use input as the assistant emitted it - `model: null` - because a `PreToolUse` rewrite happens after that record is written. The subagent's own transcript is the one that carries the applied result.

THE UNINSTALL DEFECT. `basicly-tier uninstall` removed the vendored files and left the `PreToolUse`/`Agent` entry pointing at a path that no longer existed. `install_hook.py` now carries `drop_hook`, `uninstall_claude` and a top-level `uninstall`, reached by `--uninstall`, and `kit_installer.unconfigure_host` runs it **before** deleting the files. Verified on a fresh repo from a built wheel: init wires the hook, the vendored hook resolves `haiku` for that repo's own agent, uninstall leaves **0 dangling Agent hooks** and removes the kit directory.

TWO GATES SHAPED THE SHAPE OF THE FIX. `ruff` refused a sixth parameter on `install()`, so removal is its own function rather than a `remove=` flag - which reads better anyway. `module-size` refused `tests/test_kit_install.py` at 4,195 tokens against a 4,000 cap, so the two uninstall tests live in `tests/test_kit_uninstall.py`; the cap was **not** waived.

REGRESSION TESTS. `test_uninstalling_removes_our_hook_and_leaves_a_stranger_alone` pins that an unrelated `Agent` hook written by someone else survives. `test_uninstalling_a_hook_that_was_never_installed_is_quiet` pins the no-op.

GATES. `uv run pytest -q` 5778 passed 1 xfailed. `uv run basicly verify --mode full` PASS.

STILL OPEN. Copilot has no spawn hook; that host carries per-subagent selection in config and basicly-u2hl.41 owns it. Whether a Copilot spawn honours the projected tier is unproven - only that the file loads.

STANDALONE PROVEN END TO END 2026-09-16, in a repository that has never had basicly.

A fresh `git init` directory with no `.basicly/core` and one hand-written agent file declaring `tier: low`. `uvx --from <wheel> basicly-tier init` vendored 7 files to `.basicly/kit/tier`, wrote the skill to both skill roots, and wired the `PreToolUse`/`Agent` hook. Plain `python3 .basicly/kit/tier/tier_resolver.py --host claude --name scribe` then returned `low -> haiku -> claude-haiku-4-5`, with no uv and no network.

**The spawn was then measured rather than inferred.** `claude -p` in that directory was told to spawn the `scribe` subagent once. The result object's `modelUsage`:

    claude-haiku-4-5-20251001   in=12041 out=646    <- the subagent
    claude-opus-5[1m]           in=4     out=157    <- the lead

0.1017 usd list. The lead ran Opus and the subagent ran haiku, which is what `tier: low` resolves to and what nothing else in that repository could have selected.

So all three spawn paths are now measured on claude, not one and two inferences: `claude -p` in this repository (validator, medium, sonnet), an in-session background subagent here (tester, low, haiku), and a `-p` spawn in a standalone consumer (scribe, low, haiku).

  or a short alias (`haiku`), or `inherit`.
- **GitHub Copilot** custom agents live at `.github/agents/<name>.agent.md` (org/enterprise: root
  `agents/`). Frontmatter: `description` (required), `name`, `target` (`vscode`|`github-copilot`),
  `tools`, `model`, `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`, `mcp-servers`, `metadata`; body
  capped at 30000 chars, which `agents.MAX_BODY_CHARS` already matches.
- **Copilot's `model` value is a DISPLAY NAME**, not an id - `Claude Opus 4.5`, `Claude Sonnet 4` -
  and it accepts **a single string OR a prioritized array** tried in order
  (`model: ['Claude Opus 4.5', 'GPT-5.2']`). Our schema cannot express an ordered fallback list today.
- **VS Code reads BOTH** `.github/agents` and `.claude/agents` ("VS Code also detects `.md` files in the
  `.claude/agents` folder, following the Claude sub-agents format"). So basicly-ajq's rationale holds
  for VS Code but NOT for the Copilot cloud agent or Copilot CLI, which do not read `.claude/agents`.
- Copilot `tools` names differ from Claude's and are inconsistent across sources
  (`["read","search","edit"]` in the VS Code doc vs `codebase`/`terminal`/`edit`/`github` elsewhere), so
  a copilot projection needs a pinned tool-name mapping, not a copy.

## Prerequisite

The copilot half has no target file today: basicly still projects to `.claude/agents` only. Reopening
that is filed separately and must land first for the copilot half. The claude half is unblocked once
kjc5.61 lands.

## Open design decision for the owner

Per surface, either resolve the tier to that surface's own spelling and emit it, or emit nothing and
record that the tier was not honoured (the stance kjc5.59 already takes where a family has no slot).
Recommendation: resolve and emit wherever the surface has a model slot, because that is the only case
in which the tier vocabulary changes real behaviour instead of documenting an intention.

Scope: `src/basicly/agents.py`, `.claude/agents/`, `tests/test_agents.py`.

payload.description:
## Context

Reported by the operator 2026-08-22: "I do not see any factory loop work visualization."

The page's largest region is headed `THE LOOP` and paints seven counters with progress bars: INTAKE 214, CLASSIFY 1, DECOMPOSE 19, BUILD 0, VERIFY 1, VALIDATE 0, SHIP 0.

## It is the backlog, not the loop

Measured against the live `/snapshot.json` while four lanes were building:

```text
phase histogram over units[]  : intake 215, decompose 19, build 4, verify 1, classify 1
sum                           : 240
backlog.active                : 240
```

The two are the same number because they are the same population. The region bins **every active record in the backlog** by phase. 215 of 240 sit in `intake` for the single reason that they have never been classified - `intake` is where a record is born, so the largest bar on the page measures how much of the backlog has never been touched.

Meanwhile the four lanes actually running contribute 4 to `build`, and nothing on the region distinguishes them from any other record that happens to be at that phase.

## What a loop visualization has to answer

A reader watching a factory wants to know what **this pass** is doing: which units it selected, where each one is now, which moved since the last beat, and which is stuck. None of those are answerable from a backlog histogram. The session's own selection is already on the document - `session.root`, and the lane rows - and the region does not use it.

## The counters are also not comparable

A progress bar implies a denominator. `intake` at 215 and `ship` at 0 share an axis on which 215 is not progress and 0 is not failure; they are two unrelated inventories drawn as if they were stages of one flow. A record at `intake` may never enter the loop at all.

## Context

Owner, 2026-09-02: "header is still confusing." Third time the header is raised; basicly-jbd80w and basicly-v8jwf0 moved rows and fixed the alarm band, and the owner still cannot read it. This record states what the header holds today, so the next change is against a measurement and not a feeling.

Measured on the live page at 1712x1345, three lines left and one cell right:

```text
basicly  REPO basicly · main · 1687bc87   RUN basicly-k6tpep · open · L3 [bar] 43%
GATES [GREEN] mode full · recorded 2026-09-01T19:38:28Z   SPEND machine-local · 2,032.19 usd · 36.59 usd largest · 1.4B in · 8.7M out
CLOSED TODAY not measured
                                   as of 11s ago / 2026-09-02T09:18:28Z · stale after 60s · [●] producer basicly · 0.11.0
```

Seven things a reader trips on, each verifiable against the snapshot:

1. `RUN basicly-k6tpep` is an id with no title. The snapshot's `units[]` holds the root's title; the header does not use it.
2. `L3 [bar] 43%` names no figure and no denominator. `session.spent_tokens` 42,966,175 of `token_budget` 100,000,000, and `spent_tokens_live` 55,722,904 already reads higher than the committed figure the bar uses.
3. `GATES GREEN` beside `recorded 2026-09-01T19:38:28Z` says the green is yesterday's, and nothing says whether that is fine.
4. `SPEND machine-local · 2,032.19 usd` is the lifetime spend of this machine, not the run's. It sits on the run's line and reads as the run's cost.
5. `1.4B in · 8.7M out` are lifetime token counts with no reader action attached.
6. `CLOSED TODAY not measured` is a standing row that says nothing, the shape basicly-ibzr0f removed from the cards.
7. The right cell repeats the time three ways (`as of 11s ago`, the timestamp, `stale after 60s`) and carries the boxed glyph from the sibling record.

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN the header renders, LINE ONE SHALL answer which checkout and which run: repo, branch, short head, the root's title with its id beside it, and the run status.
- WHEN a grant is live, THE HEADER SHALL print `spent of budget tokens` as two figures with the bar, using the live figure where the producer holds one and naming the committed figure as such otherwise.
- WHEN the gates cell renders, IT SHALL carry the verdict and the age of the record in the same phrase form as freshness (`recorded 14h ago`), and SHALL colour amber past the same stale threshold the freshness cell uses.
- Lifetime spend and lifetime token counts SHALL move to the footer beside `agents`, and the header SHALL carry the run's own spend only.
- A header cell whose value is `not measured` SHALL NOT render; the absence SHALL appear in the `not drawn` inventory only.
- THE freshness cell SHALL state the time once as `as of 11s ago`, keep the stale threshold, and drop the timestamp to a `title` attribute.
- `tests/test_board_render.py` SHALL assert the header cell order and the absence of `not measured` cells on the fixture.

Assumption stated: the owner named no specific confusion, so the seven items above are the ones measured on the page. The owner may strike or add items before this is dispatched.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_regions.py`
- `src/basicly/board_render.py`
- `src/basicly/board_footer.py`
- `.basicly/core/templates/board/board_page.html.j2`
- `tests/test_board_regions.py`
- `tests/test_board_render.py`
- `tests/test_board_footer.py`

payload.description:
## Trigger

When two agents work this repository in parallel and both append an event to the ledger, git reports a content conflict in `events-0001.jsonl` and one of them must hand-resolve a 9.5 MB file, so I want the append to merge cleanly on its own, so I can run lanes in parallel without a human arbitrating the log.

## Steps to Reproduce

Reproduced 2026-09-08 in a throwaway repository carrying this repo's own `.gitattributes` rule, with a positive control run immediately after.

```
printf 'events-*.jsonl -text\n' > .gitattributes
# base commit holds one event; branch agent-a appends one; branch agent-b appends one
git merge agent-b
```

Observed, exit 1:

```
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in events-0001.jsonl
{"id":"e1"}
<<<<<<< HEAD
{"id":"a1"}
=======
{"id":"b1"}
>>>>>>> agent-b
```

The control, the identical history with one word added to the rule:

```
printf 'events-*.jsonl -text merge=union\n' > .gitattributes
git merge agent-b     # exit 0, "Merge made by the 'ort' strategy"
{"id":"e1"}
{"id":"a1"}
{"id":"b1"}
```

So the conflict is the missing attribute and not the append. The control is what makes the first result a finding rather than a guess.

## Why this is the kit's central promise

The tracker kit is the part of basicly that a repository will install standalone, to replace a tracker whose records are edited in place and therefore conflict whenever two people touch the backlog. Append-only is the design that earns that, and it is already built: event ids are content-derived, `events` documents idempotency by event id as the answer to "union-merge duplication", `fsck` treats a repeated id as ordinary because "a union merge duplicates a hunk and the fold keeps one", and `provenance` states that a union merge's arbitrary concatenation folds to the same edges.

Every one of those five call sites is written for a union merge that git is never told to perform. The design is done; the one-word declaration that arms it is missing.

## What must not regress

`-text` must stay, and stay below the `*` rule. Event ids are content-derived, so a byte git rewrote on the way through the index changes an id and every later id with it (basicly-vkh0.21). `merge=union` is added beside it, never in place of it. Union must not reach `snapshot.jsonl` or any `checkpoint-*.jsonl`: those are rewritten rather than appended, and concatenating two of them yields a corrupt checkpoint. Only `events-*.jsonl` is tracked today, and the glob must stay that narrow.

## Acceptance Criteria

- THE REPOSITORY SHALL declare a union merge for the event-log glob and SHALL keep the existing `-text` attribute on it.
- THE UNION DECLARATION SHALL NOT apply to `snapshot.jsonl` or to any `checkpoint-*.jsonl`, because those are rewritten and a concatenation of two is corrupt.
- WHEN two branches each append events and are merged, THE MERGE SHALL succeed with no conflict and the result SHALL hold every event from both.
- THE FOLD OVER a union-merged log SHALL yield the same records whichever branch merged first, so the order git happens to concatenate in is not a fact about the backlog.
- THE KIT DEPLOYMENT CHECK SHALL fail where the union attribute is absent, exactly as it already fails where `-text` is absent, so the requirement cannot be lost by editing one file.
- A TEST SHALL drive the two-branch append merge end to end and assert both events survive, with a control asserting the same history conflicts when the attribute is removed.
- THE KIT SHALL install this attribute into a consumer repository that does not use basicly, since a standalone install is the case this promise is made to.

## Scope

- `.gitattributes`
- `.scripts/kit_deployment.py`
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py`
- `tests/test_kit_deployment.py`
- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`
- `changelog.d/<this-id>.fixed.md`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `130000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: build two branches that each append an event, merge them, and read every event present in the fold afterwards; then remove the attribute and watch the same merge conflict

That criterion already stands in basicly-ssbkq5c as its own line, so it is discharged there, not here. Delivered here: the attribute, the gate on both attributes, a gate on the derived files carrying no union, and an end-to-end two-branch test with a conflict control. docs/architecture/architecture.md was in scope but carries no section on the kit's host requirements to extend; the requirement lives in the kit's SPEC.md 4.4 and in .gitattributes itself.

payload.acceptance_criteria: When the design task ends, the report shall give the split of first-fold cost into fetching, walking and checking commits, and parsing events, the draft in under a page with answers to the five orchestrator questions, the verifier's breaks, the measured first-read time, shallow clone size and history-read time after one simulated year, the effect on the tracker branch candidate, and a recommendation.
payload.description:
## Context
When a new machine first reads the vault, the built fold walks and checks every commit from genesis; the spike for basicly-4z4zte8 extrapolated about 38 minutes and about 270 MiB per year of history at the owner's load. The owner asked on 2026-11-12: 'did you think about archiving? done items do not require to be read, only if explicitly required'. I want one draft design of a checkpoint commit that holds only the open records, so a normal read starts there and closed records are read only on request, with one fresh verifier and one spike, so the owner can choose between a vault repository and a tracker branch. No product code; time box 2 hours.
payload.title: Design a checkpoint that archives closed records out of the normal read

payload.text: Brief from the orchestrator 2026-11-12, from the owner's archiving idea. First answer from measurement what makes the first fold cost about 38 minutes per year: fetching, walking and checking commits, or parsing events. Idea to design and break: (1) a checkpoint commit holds a snapshot of the open records only (fields, holder, open edges); fresh segment files start after it; (2) a normal read starts at the newest checkpoint and never reads history before it; (3) done records stay in git history and are read only on explicit request; (4) a clone may be shallow down to the newest checkpoint and no deeper; the tool refuses a shallower clone; (5) any writer may write a checkpoint past a threshold; two writers race like two claims; (6) a checkpoint is valid only if its snapshot equals the fold of its parent; a full reader or fsck proves it, a shallow reader trusts it. Answer: (a) an event after a checkpoint for an archived record; (b) an open record that depends on a closed one; (c) never two holders across the boundary; (d) whether the snapshot grows without end; (e) the never-events and nothing hidden. Spike one simulated year: normal first read time, shallow clone size, one explicit history read; then what the design does to the tracker branch candidate (a period branch that restarts at a checkpoint). One draft, one fresh verifier, one spike, 2 hours, no product code; the vault hold stays.

Result 2026-11-12. Split of the built first fold (measured, 4,010 commits, 57.7 s): checking commits 97 % (cat-file of old and new segment 67 %, diff-tree 15 %), walking (rev-list per commit) 14 %, local fetch 0.8 %, parsing 0.3 %; 10.8 to 14.4 ms per commit, growing as segments fill. Spike, one full simulated year (250 days, 210,935 commits, 299,254 events, 59 checkpoints every 5,000 events), measured: normal first read 17.7 s at the tip and 22.7 s worst case, against about 38 minutes for a full fold (extrapolated); clone shallow to the newest checkpoint 1.2 to 1.4 MiB; checkpoint.json 74 to 103 KiB, 167 to 234 open records; one explicit history read 8.3 s unshallow (84.6 MiB) plus 7.8 s search, or about 1 s after the fetch using the closed ids in checkpoint messages; whole vault 114 MiB size-pack (generator differs from the baseline, so the drop is not all from checkpoints; checkpoints alone saved about 21 % at 20 days). Tracker branch E with a period branch: 1.36 MiB of tracker objects in a default clone against 97.7 MiB for the full branch, but old periods then live only under a custom ref (refs/tracker-archive/*), which is a git ref outside branches, the hidden storage the owner banned; under a tag they come back into every clone; with no ref they are pruned. Verifier on draft 1: fail with 5 fixable breaks (a depth refetch false retraction and repair replay giving two holders; no create or restore in the fold; built shape rules quarantine a checkpoint and quarantine is a skip; fold_digest separate from the snapshot and no comparer when alone; the depth from commit text is untrusted) and 1 nit. Recommendation: the checkpoint design holds with those fixes; build it after the basicly cutover, as a slice of about 5 hours, plus a 1 to 2 hour batching of git calls in the fold.

payload.description:
§9/§11.8: let a consumer choose a subset of the catalog at install time. Design settled 2026-07-16 (see comment): technology scoping — sources carry an optional `technologies:` list (absent = universal, always ships); install records the repo's selection in `basicly.toml` (default: all); projection commands filter unselected sources and the manifest sweep removes outputs a narrowed selection excludes; core sync stays full. Tag vocabulary is a controlled list enforced by catalog-lint. v2 (out of scope): per-block technology conditioning inside agent slots.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Catalog sources (skills, fragments, agents-fragments, hooks) accept an optional `technologies:` list; a source without it is universal and always projected
- catalog-lint rejects a `technologies:` value outside the controlled vocabulary (stack tags like python/go plus environment tools like zsh/tmux/starship/wezterm)
- `basicly install` accepts a technology-selection flag and records the selection in `basicly.toml`; omitting it selects everything (current behavior unchanged)
- `basicly build` / `skills-build` / `agents-build` / `hooks-build` skip sources whose `technologies:` has no overlap with the recorded selection; core sync still copies the full catalog
- Narrowing the selection then rebuilding sweeps the now-excluded projections via the manifest (no stale outputs left)
- A repo with no selection recorded in `basicly.toml` projects the full catalog (backward compatible)
- Regression tests cover: universal source always ships, tagged source filtered out, selection recorded/read from basicly.toml, sweep after narrowing, lint rejection of unknown tags
- docs/architecture.md documents the property, the selection, and the filtering point

payload.description:
Measured on basicly 0.21.5 (basicly-tracker 0.2.1) on 2026-10-09, in a beads (br) migration. The import promises to keep source ids, so that a commit message that cites an old id still resolves. The id dev-memory-audit-multi-target-2zx had to be renamed, and its citations in git history no longer resolve.

Cause: ids.py RECORD_ID_PATTERN is [a-z][a-z0-9]*-[a-z0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)*. It allows no hyphen after the prefix. br create --slug mints exactly such ids.

Reproduction:
1. br 0.3.2 in a scratch repo: br init --prefix dev; br create probe --slug memory-audit-multi-target --json. Observed id: dev-memory-audit-multi-target-ner.
2. A beads JSONL record {"id": "dev-memory-audit-multi-target-2zx", "issue_type": "task", ...}; basicly-tracker import <ledger> <export> (tag v0.21.5).
Observed: rejected, reason "not a record id".

Expected: the import accepts every id that beads mints, or it maps the id and keeps the old id as a searchable alias.
payload.title: Import refuses a valid beads slug id

payload.description:
## Trigger

When a person uses the tracker in many repositories, I want the kit code installed once per machine and only the ledger in each repository, with a single vendored file as the fallback for a person who wants a sandbox per repository, so I can upgrade the tracker in one place without losing a pinned, gated setup.

## Context

Owner decision 2026-09-25: option A (code once per machine, data per repository) is the default, and option B (one vendored tracker.pyz per repository, 356 KB, from basicly-tracker bundle) is the uncomplicated fallback. Measured on v0.18.9: basicly-tracker passes every kit verb through; the tracker skill names python3 .basicly/kit/tracker/cli.py 14 times; the commit-msg hook skips the claim check when that file is absent; SPEC 331 lets an older reader only warn on an unknown event kind, so version skew loses facts silently. The basicly engine stays per repository and is out of scope.
payload.requirements: One resolution rule, read by every caller: the repository's pyz when present, else the user-level command, always at the version the repository pins; a missing or mismatched tracker refuses with the fix, never skips.

payload.description:
## Trigger

When the tracker install offers to import a backlog from beads or beans, I want the storage layout, record format, id shape and detection markers of bd, br and beans established from their own sources, so I can build detection and import on facts rather than recall.

## Context

Read 2026-09-25 by a researcher from primary sources.

- bd (steveyegge/beads, now gastownhall/beads, main 3c30a28d, release v1.3.0): the store is Dolt under .beads/embeddeddolt or .beads/dolt, not committed. .beads/issues.jsonl is an optional export, off by default (export.auto false); bd export writes JSONL to stdout or -o FILE. Markers: .beads/metadata.json, .beads/config.yaml, .beads/dolt or embeddeddolt. Statuses open, in_progress, blocked, deferred, closed, pinned, hooked. Parent links are parent-child dependency edges. Comment id is a string.
- br (Dicklesworthstone/beads_rust, main 565b43c8, release v0.7.0; installed br is 0.3.2): SQLite .beads/beads.db is local; .beads/issues.jsonl is the committed interchange file. No br export: br sync --flush-only writes it. Markers: .beads/ with metadata.json naming jsonl_export, config.yaml (issue_prefix), beads.db. Extra statuses draft, tombstone. Comment id is an integer. br writes absolute paths in source_repo_path, so an import must scrub it.
- bd and br share the core fields and the dependency edge shape {issue_id, depends_on_id, type, created_at, created_by, metadata, thread_id} that our importer already reads (migrate.py).
- beans (hmans/beans, main 99260bf1, release v0.4.2): .beans.yml at the root plus one committed Markdown file per bean under .beans/ and .beans/archive/, file name id--slug.md. YAML frontmatter keys title, status, type, priority, tags, created_at, updated_at, order, parent, blocking, blocked_by; the body is the Markdown after the frontmatter; the id comes from the file name. Statuses in-progress, todo, draft, completed, scrapped; types milestone, epic, bug, feature, task; priorities critical, high, normal, low, deferred. No export command; beans list --json --full gives JSON with the same keys.
- Not established: a real bd export line with edges and comments; the br 0.7.0 flag list; how bd deletes; the beans GraphQL schema.

Three assumptions carry large downstream work and each has a cheap test; at least one could cancel a whole phase. 1a (recall) is independent and can run first. 1b (7bur, cost per landed package) is the hub - the design documents defer four further decisions to it, and kjc5.29 must land first so tier economics are not measured against an unpinned model mapping. 1c (localisation) must precede Phase 5 because it changes what the decomposer scope declarations have to carry.

payload.value:
## Context

Plan §4 Phase 1. Depends on Phase 0 for 1b and 1c. Size 3-4 sessions.

Three assumptions carry large downstream work and each has a cheap test; at least one could cancel a whole phase. 1a (recall) is independent and can run first. 1b (7bur, cost per landed package) is the hub - the design documents defer four further decisions to it, and kjc5.29 must land first so tier economics are not measured against an unpinned model mapping. 1c (localisation) must precede Phase 5 because it changes what the decomposer scope declarations have to carry.

Risk: 1b is a genuine build, not a measurement script, and is the item most likely to slip. Hard constraint carried over - the eval must not cost more than the thing it measures.

## Success Criteria

- Each of the three Phase 1 measurements carries a number, its method and its date on the record that owns it, and the document that consumes it cites that record rather than restating an estimate: recall against a no-guidance control (`basicly-agzx.1`, closed), localisation effect on pre-first-edit tokens (`basicly-agzx.2`), conditional-relevance effect on adherence (`basicly-agzx.3`).
- Cost per landed package is answerable from run records rather than forecast. `basicly-agzx.4` (closed) recorded that the cost record carried no forecast in 92 percent of landed units; the criterion is that the same query re-run returns a figure for the current population, and that the figure is what the roster tier table is decided on.
- The 1b hub is reachable from this epic. `basicly-7bur` is the cost-per-landed-package instrument this epic's context names as 1b, and it is not a child of this epic - it hangs off `basicly-kjc5` and blocks `basicly-u6jq` and `basicly-s2xf`. Either it is re-parented here or this epic's context stops claiming it.
- The eval costs less than the work it measures, stated as two token totals drawn from the same ledger rather than as an assurance.
- The localisation question is decided before Phase 5 decomposes: `basicly-agzx.2`'s verdict is on the record, and the decomposer's scope-declaration requirement is changed or explicitly left alone as a recorded consequence of it.

payload.description:
## Context

`humanlayer/skills` `improve-claude-md` (**MIT**) claims Claude Code's system reminder -
this context may or may not be relevant - makes the model ignore parts of a CLAUDE.md, and
proposes wrapping conditional guidance in `<important if="condition">` blocks.

## Why this is ours to test and not to assume

We measured **recall**: 98% claude, 93% copilot (`basicly-agzx.1`). Their claim is about
**adherence**. Those are different quantities, and this repo's own standing rule is that
recall is an upper bound that may not be cited as evidence of quality. So our data neither
supports nor refutes them, and we have the instrument - `.scripts/recall_eval.py` plus the
path-scoped tier - that would settle it.

## Two constraints on the answer

1. **Claude root only.** `<important if>` is Claude-specific XML, and `basicly-a3ab.5`
   forbids one target's instruction file naming another target's enforcement mechanism. If
   it wins it becomes a projection detail in `.claude/rules/`, never `AGENTS.md`.
2. **The premise is an assertion about a vendor's internals.** Per the `interface-facts`
   rule, check the vendor's current documentation for what it says about instruction
   weighting before attributing a mechanism to the result. A measured difference with no
   explanation is still a finding; a claimed mechanism is not.

## Also adopt regardless of the outcome

Two portable rules from the same source, neither Claude-specific: cut any instruction a gate
can enforce, and cut code snippets in favour of file-path references. Both belong in
`basicly-a3ab.1`'s baseline audit.

## Scope

- `.scripts/recall_eval.py`
- `.basicly/core/fragments/**`
- `tests/**`

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- budget: `90000`
- depends on: none

payload.description:
## Context

The cost rollup under-reports a landed unit, and the shortfall is one whole dispatch rather than a rounding difference. Measured on basicly-vkh0.27 the day it landed, 2026-08-17, from the owned ledger.

The unit's own [harness-cost] record:

    {"actual": {"cost": 11.7265305, "dispatches": 1, "estimated": false, "rework": 0,
                "tokens": 15810802, "wall_clock_s": 1567.63111574},
     "forecast": {"cost": null, "tokens": null, "wall_clock_s": null},
     "scope_tokens": null, "task_class": "task"}

The same unit's [harness-run] records, three of them:

    run-921dfc68e1 phase=build   15810802 tokens
    run-3baf1603bf phase=ship     1780766 tokens
    run-3baf1603bf-2 phase=ship   1793781 tokens

So `tokens` in the cost record is the build run alone, and `dispatches: 1` counts one of three. The sum of build plus the first ship run is 17591568, which reconciles exactly with the grant ledger's own delta across the lane: 51102083 minus 33510515. Two independent instruments agree on 17591568; the cost record says 15810802, which is 10.1 percent low against the grant and 18.5 percent low against all three runs.

The `cost` figure of 11.73 US dollars is presumably build-only for the same reason, and nothing in the record says so.

## Why it matters

Cost per landed unit is the instrument the tier claims rest on. An instrument that silently drops the ship phase makes every landed unit look cheaper than it was, and the error is not constant: it scales with how much ship work a unit needs.

Two further gaps in the same record, both visible above: `forecast` is null on all three fields for a unit that was forecast at preflight, and `scope_tokens` is null although the bead declares a scope. So forecast against actual cannot be computed for this landing at all, which is the comparison the record exists to support.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cost_rollup.py`
- `tests/test_cost_rollup.py`

Given the same unit then dispatches equals the number of run records, not the number of phases and not one
Given a unit whose runs are known then the recorded token total reconciles with the grant ledger delta across the same unit
Given the cost figure covers fewer runs than the unit holds then the record says which runs it covers rather than reporting a bare number

payload.name: description
payload.value:
## Context

Cost per landed unit is the instrument the tier claims rest on, and it is not recording what it claims to. Two defects, measured 2026-08-17 over all 202 cost records in the owned ledger. The second is the headline; the first is what led to it.

## 1 · The forecast is absent from 185 of 202 records, which is 91.6 percent

`[harness-cost]` exists to carry a forecast beside the actual it produced. In 185 of 202 records `forecast.tokens` is null, and `scope_tokens` is null with it, so forecast against actual cannot be computed for that population at all.

The cause is a content-key miss and not a missing write. `cost_rollup.record` calls `decompose.forecast_for(repo_root, task_class, scope)`, which builds a key from the work type plus the globs and then searches the export for a frozen sizing marker under that key. The estimate is frozen on the feature, priced over its **working set**; the rollup looks it up with the bead's **ownership scope**. Different globs give a different key, so the lookup misses and returns None. `forecast_for`'s own docstring predicts exactly this: "A caller holding only the ownership scope therefore misses on a bead declaring its own `## Working Set`, and gets a null rather than a forecast over the wrong material."

The population supports it: the ledger holds 35 sizing markers against 202 cost records.

Probe, reproducible on any bead:

    decompose.forecast_for(repo_root, *decompose.bead_class_and_scope(repo_root, 'basicly-vkh0.29'))  ->  None

## 2 · The curator's dispatch is never in the total, in the units that had one

On basicly-vkh0.27 the cost record says `dispatches: 1, tokens: 15810802` while the unit holds three run records: build 15810802, ship 1780766, ship 1793781. Build plus the first ship run is 17591568, which reconciles exactly with the grant ledger's delta over the same lane, 51102083 minus 33510515. Two independent instruments agree on 17591568 and the cost record is 10.1 percent below it.

The cause is ordering, and it is structural rather than intermittent: `loop._on_ship` calls `cost_rollup.record` at line 641 and `_dispatch_curation` at line 642. The rollup is written before the curator has spent anything, and it cannot simply move later because the comment above it records why it must precede `merge.commit_tracker_state` - a marker written after that commit sits in the local database only.

**The undercount is bounded, not universal.** Of 202 units, 194 agree with their run count and 8 do not: e2mz.16 (3 against 6), vkh0.27 (1 against 3), e2mz.13 (3 against 4), vkh0.26, vkh0.28, e2mz.30 and two more at one run each. None over-counts. The 194 agree because curation is skipped under the supervisor's landing pass, so most units have no ship dispatch to miss. An earlier draft of this bead claimed the shortfall was general; the measurement above refuted it.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cost_rollup.py`
- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `tests/test_cost_rollup.py`

Given a landed unit with no frozen estimate then the record says so rather than carrying a bare null
Given a unit that ran a curator at ship then the recorded dispatch count and token total include that run
Given the whole ledger then no cost record reports fewer dispatches than the unit holds run records
Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_cost_rollup.py -q

payload.text:
Correcting my own close. I closed this bead when three of its four acceptance criteria were met; the third - that a unit which ran a curator at ship has that run in its recorded dispatch count and token total - was not. It needed src/basicly/loop.py, which a live lane held at the time, and I closed anyway.

It landed in 1f3162b. loop._on_ship called cost_rollup.record and then _dispatch_curation, so the curator - which is a dispatch - could never be in the rollup it precedes. The two are now swapped, which keeps the constraint that mattered: the rollup still precedes merge.commit_tracker_state, because a marker written after that commit sits in the local database only.

Proven to discriminate rather than asserted: with the old order restored the new test fails, with the fix in place it passes, and the assertion is the order list ["curate", "rollup", "close", "commit"] rather than a count, because the count is what the order decides.

The measured symptom that started it: basicly-wpc8.1 recorded dispatches: 1 while its own ledger held two ship-phase run records at 1780766 and 1793781 tokens.

payload.description:
## Context

`basicly worktree merge` takes a worktree name and merges whatever its branch points at **now**. There
is no way to say which commits were expected, and the report names the merge commit rather than the
branch tip it took.

This cost real work on 2026-08-20. An agent finished and reported its commit; a follow up message was
sent to it, which **resumed it**; it did another 92 lines and committed again; the merge then took the
tip that had been read earlier. Nothing in the landing said the tip had moved. It was caught only by a
routine `git diff <branch> main` run before cleanup, which showed main *removing* 92 lines, and the
commit was recovered by cherry pick.

The general defect: a landing is the one irreversible step, and it is the step with no statement of
intent to check against. An `--expect <sha>` that refuses a mismatch, or a report that names the tip and
the commit count it is about to take, closes it. The second is cheaper and helps even when no sha is
known in advance.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a worktree, commit on it, and note the branch tip.
2. Commit again on the branch without re-reading the tip.
3. Run `basicly worktree merge <name> --bead <id>`.
4. Observe the report names the resulting merge commit and never the branch tip it took or how many commits it took.
5. Observe there is no flag by which the operator could have declared the tip they expected.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a landing when it merges then its report names the branch tip it took and the number of commits it carried - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_merge.py -k names_the_tip -q`
- Given an expected tip is declared and the branch has moved then the landing refuses naming both shas rather than merging

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/worktree.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/worktree.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_merge.py -k names_the_tip -q`
payload.title: a landing merges whatever the branch points at with no way to state what was expected

## Trigger

When a consumer finds a record under a parent that the record type rule does not allow, I want to move it under another parent or to the top level, so I can bring the ledger in line with the rule without re-creating the record.

## Evidence

handily, 2026-10-14, record handily-fwkt.18: the epics handily-fwkt.2, handily-fwkt.8 and handily-fwkt.9 sit under the epic handily-fwkt, which the rule refuses (record_types.py CHILD_TYPES: an epic sits under no record). tracker undep refuses their edge: a parent-child edge is not retractable, because removing it re-parents the record while its id still spells its parent, so re-parenting needs its own verb. basicly 0.23.1 has no such verb. Today a retype of such a record is refused, and the record stays out of rule.

## Scope

The tracker kit: a re-parent verb, the id rule for a moved record, the type rule check on the new parent, and its tests.

Gap (user, 2026-07-16): basicly projects fragments, skills, and hooks — but not agent files. Subagent definitions (.claude/agents/*.md) are hand-authored per repo with no single source of truth, so they drift and cannot be centrally improved.

Vision: agent files become generated artifacts composed by the projector from an essential-blocks taxonomy (candidate blocks: security, planning, git, orchestration, conventions, documentation, hygiene, hardening, enforcement, verify, validate, authorize, authenticate, context, work tracking, work scoping, review, gates). Core blocks are owned by basicly devs; consumers extend or override specific blocks with custom building blocks via the .basicly-local overlay — the same core/overlay model fragments already use. Generated agent files carry the generated marker, are gated by protect-generated, and must never be edited manually.

Emission is single-source per the 2f4 policy: .claude/agents/ only — VS Code parses the Claude sub-agent format natively (user-shared research finding, 2026-07-16), and Claude Code reads only .claude/.

Prerequisite research: the 84v SOTA research covered instruction-file blocks, not subagent-file anatomy. A dedicated research pass (Anthropic sub-agents spec + VS Code custom-agent docs + curated corpus: awesome-claude-code, VoltAgent/awesome-claude-code-subagents, wshobson/agents) must establish the frontmatter contract, the recurring body anatomy, and a frequency-ranked block taxonomy before the schema is designed. Findings land as comments on this bead.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Research findings recorded on this bead: frontmatter contract, cross-tool field compatibility, body anatomy, ranked building-block taxonomy mapped to the candidate list
- New agents catalog kind: YAML sources in .basicly/core (schema + catalog-lint coverage + scaffold command consistent with skills-new/fragment-new)
- Projector composes and renders .claude/agents/*.md with the generated marker; protect-generated blocks manual edits
- Overlay can add whole agents and extend/override individual blocks of core agents
- basicly check/build/install/uninstall handle the new kind (manifest-tracked, stale-file sweep)
- docs/architecture.md documents the kind, the composition model, and the single-source emission policy
- Tests cover schema validation, composition/override precedence, rendering, and the sweep
